extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges (readers of a legal treatise on patent law)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating patent novelty and public use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining novelty, inventorship, public use, abandonment, and prior-user/purchaser rights under 19th-century U.S./English patent law and related statutes (notably the Acts of 1836 and 1839). Focuses on when prior experiments, uses, suggestions, servants' contributions, or sales defeat or preserve patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment versus completed invention (presumption from abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention has not been completed, but rests in experiment and trial, acts done earlier may be only experimental and not constitute a complete invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a presumption that long periods of inactivity (e.g., twenty or thirty years) after experiments indicate the matter remained experimental and was abandoned; conversely, continued experiments or lack of satisfactory evidence of abandonment makes it a question of fact whether the inventor had accomplished the same substantial result as described in the patent. Consider nature of proposed invention, character of experiments, and results attained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior public use when invention was already completed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior actor had a completed invention that was publicly used long before the plaintiff's patent, that prior use can defeat novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prior use is of the same thing 'in substance' and openly used so all could see it and continued up to time of taking out the patent, then the later patent is not new and is invalid. However, whether an earlier device was merely experimental or a completed invention is a factual question for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requires actual invention or discovery by claimant
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of every patent must have been 'invented or discovered' by the party claiming to be the inventor or discoverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many suggestions or hints may have been used by an inventor, but the law intends to protect the intellectual production when perfected into a thing differing from others by some substantial peculiarity (i.e., the perfected, practically-operable invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection applies to perfected invention, not mere abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The law protects the perfected invention — the idea applied to a practical purpose and made capable of useful operation — not the mere abstract suggestion or inchoate idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long interval between first suggestion and actual production may involve inventive work; the extent of that inventive work determines who is inventor. The person who first applies and reduces the idea to practical operation ordinarily is the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of proving only a 'naked idea' from another
rubrics_metrics.description: To invalidate a patent on the ground that the patentee received the suggestion from another, it is not enough to show that the naked idea or bare possibility was suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must appear that the invention was substantially communicated to the patentee so that, without more inventive power, he could have applied it in practice. Conversely, minutiae need not have been communicated; substantial communication is the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person who perfects and reduces to practice is inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Although others may have previously had the idea and made some experiments, the person who first brought the machine to perfection and made it capable of useful operation is the inventor and entitled to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English law may allow using antecedent experiments of others in perfecting an invention; U.S. law is similar in principle though historically not always to the same extent. Prior incomplete experiments of others do not vitiate a subsequent inventor's patent if he perfects the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer vs servant: who is inventor depends on facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an employer or a servant is to be regarded as the inventor depends on the relative situations, nature of employment, and whether the employer planned or conceived the main idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the servant suggests the principle of the invention, the servant is the inventor. If the employer conceived the general idea and employed the servant merely to realize mechanical details (even requiring manual dexterity or inventive skill), the employer may be the inventor and the servant a mere instrument. Each case depends on its own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of trivial suggestions by workmen usually not fatal to patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption by an inventor of suggestions made in the course of experiments (e.g., conveniences suggested by workmen) does not necessarily affect validity of the patent when the principle and object of the invention are complete without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial or convenience suggestions that do not touch the principle of the invention are unlikely to render a patent void; courts consider whether such suggestions form important parts of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of use of antecedent experiments by later inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent experiments of others, not carried to completion, will not vitiate the patent of a more successful person who perfects the invention and avails himself of knowledge gained by predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The later inventor may use the results of prior experiments in perfecting his invention; mere speculative or uncompleted trials by others do not bar the later patent if the later inventor brings it to practical operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule (Act of 1836): no patent if subject was in public use or on sale with patentee's consent at time of application
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires that the subject of the patent should not have been, at the time of the application, in public use or on sale with the consent or allowance of the patentee as inventor or discoverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A voluntary public sale or use with the inventor's knowledge before application creates a disability to comply with statutory terms and renders the patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'public use' (use in public, not 'by the public')
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'public use' means use in public, and not use by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a device where the public might see it, manufacture and sale without secrecy, or publicly making and selling articles according to a model retained are examples of public use that vitiate subsequent letters patent. Whether use is a public use is a question for the jury, depending on evidence as to manufacturing and visibility vs mere experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use must be of a completed subject substantially as patented
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat a patent, the machine or other subject must have been completed and used in public substantially as it was patented, with the consent of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental or tentative uses that do not amount to the completed invention or are undertaken to test utility are not the same as public use that defeats a patent; courts look to whether the use was substantially the same as the patented invention and was permitted by the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of pre-1839 public use that could void patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to 1839, an inventor might allow public use in two modes that would void a patent: (1) permitted use in public by an individual or individuals; or (2) dedication/abandonment of the invention to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting use to an individual had to be unlimited in time or object to be fatal; limited permission for a short or definite period, or for further experiments, did not necessarily defeat a patent under the Act of 1836. Dedication/abandonment required very clear and cogent circumstances to be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication/abandonment to the public requires unequivocal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's acts must be very clear and cogent to establish that he has dedicated or abandoned his invention to the public prior to application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe inventors' acts liberally in the inventor's favor; yet unequivocal conduct proclaiming intent to the world and permitting general public use without objection can be strong proof of abandonment and will deprive the inventor of later patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1839 (ch. 88 §7) — prior purchaser/user protection and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1839 Act provides that persons or corporations who purchased or constructed a newly invented machine, manufacture, or composition prior to the inventor's application shall have the right to use and vend the specific machine so made or purchased without liability; and no patent shall be held invalid by reason of such prior purchase, sale, or use except on proof of abandonment or that such prior use/purchase was for more than two years prior to application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relieves purchasers who, with the inventor's consent or allowance, had prior use, placing them on the footing of licensees. The patent remains valid against all others after issue, but earlier purchasers retain the right to use what they purchased. The statute does not protect purchasers from wrong-doers (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to claim benefit of the 1839 purchaser/user protection
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the benefit of the statute, the person must have been a purchaser or have used the invention before the patent was issued by license, grant, or consent of the inventor, and must not be a purchaser under a mere wrong-doer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not allow a wrong-doer who pirated an invention to confer a valid right on subsequent purchasers; the statute contemplates purchasers/users who obtained machines legitimately (e.g., with consent/licence), not bona fide purchasers from someone who lacked title to confer it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year grace/limit for prior permitted use by individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may permit use of the invention by individuals for up to two years prior to application and still obtain a valid patent; if such permitted use extends for more than two years prior to application, or amounts to abandonment to the public, the patent will be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-year limitation is statutory (Act of 1839); courts examine whether prior use was with inventor's consent and whether use exceeded the statutory period or constituted dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee patents where inventor employed and paid for another's inventive faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee employed and paid for the inventive faculty of another, the patentee may claim and hold a patent for the invention not as the inventor but as the assignee of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category of cases concerns assignments and is distinguishable from determining who the actual inventor is; assignment law and employment arrangements govern whether the employer or payor holds rights as assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of public use or sale as statutory disability rather than mere intent
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or use with the inventor's knowledge or consent before application creates a legal inference (statutory disability) affecting the public, not merely a question of inventor's subjective intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervening sale/use between application and grant is not within the act and does not create the disabling presumption; the key is conduct before application. Whether acts constitute abandonment or dedication is typically a question of fact for the jury.
